Inseparable phrasal verbs, watch out for, count on

A phrasal verb is the combination of a verb with a preposition or adverb (or both) that that has a meaning that is different from each of the words that are part of the verb. In other words, its meaning is hard to get at a first glance.

There are two types of phrasal verbs separable and inseparable phrasal verbs. Separable phrasal verbs can be separated by other words, while inseparable phrasal verbs cannot be separated by other words.

Inseparable phrasal verbs can be transitive, which means they can take a direct object, but you cannot place that direct object in the middle of the phrasal verb. In other words, they cannot be split, That is where their name come from. Here we are going to take a look at two of this kind of verbs:

  • Watch out for (something or someone): to be careful or cautious
    Watch out for the viruses on that web page.
  • Count on (something or someone): to rely or depend on 
    You can count on me to make this database model.
Today you can count on me to clarify all your doubts and questions regarding this topic.
Next, you need to watch out for the entity sets and the keys that work together.
Cardinality is the relationship between one data table and another.

To map cardinality you need to define the kind of relationship existing between entities in given sets.

The cardinalities can be:

  • One to one: an entity or entities from a set can be linked with other entity in another set.
  • One to many: one entity from an entity set can be associated to more than one entity in another entity set.
  • Many to one: more than one entity from an entity set can be related to only one entity in another entity set.
  • Many to many: one entity from an entity set can be related to many entities in another entity set and vice versa.

The ER model for the database management system can be complicated and difficult to understand. Today you can count on me to clarify all your doubts and questions regarding this topic. </br></br>
The ER model is based on some simple elements you should have very clear. The first element to check is the entity. An entity is a piece of information that can be easily distinguishable, it can be part or not of the real world. Then, we have the attribute. The attributes are the characteristics that define each entity.

There are several kinds of attributes: the simple attribute, which are atomic values that cannot be divided further; the composite attribute, which are made of more than one attribute; the derived attribute, which are attributes that do not exist in the physical database but are derived from other attributes; the single value attribute, which contain a single value; and the multi-value attribute, which may contain more than one attributes. These kinds of attributes make each reference to the different ways values can be part of the attributes. </br></br>
Next, you need to watch out for the entity sets and the keys that work together. An entity set is a group of related types of entities, and a key is an attribute that distinguishes one particular (unique) entity from the set. There are three types of keys: the superkey, a candidate key, and a primary key.

Without the ER model, the DBMS could not work, and it is here when the relationships become important. A relationship is a way two entities are related. There are three types of relationships the binary, the ternary and the n-ary. As you can see the number of participants in the relationships is what defines the type of relationship. </br></br>To wrap things up, I would like to go very quickly over the cardinalities, which are the different way that entity sets are associated. Cardinalities can be one to one, one to many, many to one or many to many.
